summary: A 1969 note making two suggestions for reducing congestion at hosts that swap programs in and out of memory. One is to let the host control the order in which the IMP delivers messages, so it does not waste time swapping a user out and in. It is a proposal, not a standard.

eli5.summary: A busy teacher can only talk to one student at a time. This note suggests letting the teacher choose who to hear next so there is less shuffling around.

questions: reduce congestion at swap bound nodes
how did early arpanet hosts handle congestion
subtitle: Let hosts choose which messages to receive first to reduce swapping overhead.

tldr.problem: Hosts with limited memory swap programs in and out of core constantly. When messages arrive out of convenient order, the host wastes time swapping.
tldr.mechanism: Two proposals: let the host read the IMP's message queue and accept messages in the order that minimizes swapping, or lock programs in core during multi-message transfers.
tldr.outcome: The proposals were not adopted into the core network protocols, but later systems explored similar congestion-reduction techniques.

today: These protocol modifications were not adopted, and the early ARPANET evolved different congestion-control approaches.

sections.title: The Congestion Problem
sections.content: Early ARPANET hosts varied widely in their ability to swap data between core memory and auxiliary storage. Slower systems like the SDC 360/50 could improve network utility by changing how messages arrive from the IMP. When the IMP delivers messages in a fixed order, a host with limited core memory might waste time swapping programs in and out to process messages in an inconvenient sequence.
sections.eli5: When messages come to a slow computer in the wrong order, it has to keep swapping programs around, wasting time.

sections.title: HOST Control of Message Ordering
sections.content: The first proposal is HOST control of message ordering. If the HOST could read the IMP's queue of waiting messages and accept them in the order it finds most effective, it could avoid wasteful swapping. For example, if the IMP has messages for timeshare users A and B in that order, but user B is currently in core, the HOST could accept B's message first, avoiding a swap. This would require changes to the IMP-HOST protocol and BBN's IMP software.
sections.eli5: Let the host say which message it wants next instead of taking them in order. That avoids having to swap programs in and out.

sections.title: Core-to-Core Transfers
sections.content: The second proposal is core-to-core transfers between HOSTS with locked programs. Cooperating hosts could agree to lock appropriate programs in core for the duration of a multi-message file transfer on an auxiliary connection. This could greatly reduce the time to transfer files to and from a swap-bound HOST. However, the practical limits are severe: at 50 kilobit/sec with 100% efficiency, this yields only about 6 8-kilobit messages per second. Locking a program in core for more than 2 seconds may be unacceptable in a timeshare environment, making this approach practical only for file sizes of 2 to 16 messages.
sections.eli5: Keep programs locked in memory during big file transfers so they do not have to swap. But this only works for smaller files.
